attribution_limitations: The article text says the electrophysiological study induced polymorphic ventricular tachycardia terminated by cardioversion, while the Figure 2 caption says ventricular fibrillation was induced, sustained and terminated by a 360-J transthoracic direct current shock.
ST elevation is given as greater than 2 mm in the text but as 2 mm in the Figure 1 caption (likely rounding or wording).
The abstract calls the epilepsy "presumed idiopathic" while the case text and discussion state idiopathic epilepsy and an epilepsy diagnosis.

The source does not say whether the "most recent admission" (seizure with lorazepam) and the "initial admission" used as the anchor for lamotrigine discontinuation and the 3-month follow-up are the same admission.
Levetiracetam was previously prescribed before lamotrigine was introduced and is currently received; the source does not state whether it was continued throughout or stopped and restarted.
The EEG stimulation is worded "phonic stimulation" in the source (possibly photic); wording kept literal.

After the ICD recommendation and discussion the source says the patient "refused further treatment"; the ICD is recorded as declined on that wording, without a sentence naming the ICD as the refused item.

claims.text: A 27-year-old man with a 4-year history of idiopathic epilepsy, previously on levetiracetam, was referred to cardiology for recurrent syncopal episodes and an abnormal electrocardiogram. Syncope began after lamotrigine was introduced; ECGs before lamotrigine showed normal sinus rhythm without a type 1 Brugada pattern. His most recent admission was for a generalized tonic-clonic seizure terminated with intravenous lorazepam; a baseline emergency department ECG showed V1 and V2 ST elevation, a prominent J wave and negative T waves: a type 1 Brugada pattern.

Repeat ECGs were consistent with a type 1 Brugada pattern. A positive electrophysiological study with programmed stimulation of the right ventricular outflow tract induced a ventricular arrhythmia that was terminated by cardioversion. The authors attribute the unmasking of Brugada syndrome to lamotrigine.
